[1] PostgreSQL: Release Notes
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/17.0
* New memory management system for `VACUUM`, which reduces memory consumption and can improve overall vacuuming performance. * New SQL/JSON capabilities, including constructors, identity functions, and the `JSON_TABLE()` function, which converts JSON data into a table representation. + pg\_upgrade now preserves logical replication slots on publishers and full subscription state on subscribers. This will allow upgrades to future major versions to continue logical replication without requiring copy to resynchronize. * `COPY` adds a new option, `ON_ERROR ignore`, that allows a copy operation to continue in the event of an error. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 17 are explained in more detail in the sections below. A dump/restore using pg\_dumpall or use of pg\_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. The new behavior is based on the session user's superuser status at the time the `SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION` command is issued, rather than their superuser status at connection time.

[4] PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL 17 Released!
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-17-released-2936
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 17, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database. This release of PostgreSQL adds significant overall performance gains, including an overhauled memory management implementation for vacuum, optimizations to storage access and improvements for high concurrency workloads, speedups in bulk loading and exports, and query execution improvements for indexes. PostgreSQL 17 has features that benefit brand new workloads and critical systems alike, such as additions to the developer experience with the SQL/JSON `JSON_TABLE` command, and enhancements to logical replication that simplify management of high availability workloads and major version upgrades. PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from over 25 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.

content.text:
The headline index-related change in PostgreSQL 17 is an improvement to how B-tree indexes handle queries with multiple values — specifically `IN (...)` lists and `= ANY(...)` conditions.

Before 17, if you had a query like `WHERE id IN (1, 5, 200, 9000)`, the planner would often do a separate index descent for each value. In 17, the B-tree code can process the whole set of values in a single index scan, which cuts down on repeated tree traversals and buffer accesses. For queries scanning many values against a large index, this is a real speedup.

The other relevant one is on the maintenance side: `VACUUM` got an overhauled memory management system for tracking dead tuples. That doesn't change how indexes *serve* queries, but it makes vacuuming (which includes cleaning up index entries) faster and less memory-hungry — which indirectly keeps your indexes healthier and your query performance more predictable.

There were also some improvements to BRIN indexes allowing parallel builds.

Is there one of these you want to dig into? The B-tree `IN`-list change is the one most likely to show up in your actual `EXPLAIN` plans, so if you're trying to understand why a query got faster, that's where I'd focus.

key_takeaways: PostgreSQL 17's headline index change improves B-tree handling of multi-value queries: conditions like `WHERE id IN (1, 5, 200, 9000)` or `= ANY(...)` can now be processed in a single index scan rather than a separate index descent per value, reducing repeated tree traversals and buffer accesses.
This B-tree IN-list improvement is the change most likely to show up directly in `EXPLAIN` plans and to explain observed query speedups on large indexes.

PostgreSQL 17 introduced a new VACUUM memory management system that reduces memory consumption and speeds up vacuuming; this doesn't change how indexes serve queries but indirectly keeps indexes healthier and query performance more predictable via faster cleanup of dead index entries.
PostgreSQL 17 also added support for parallel builds of BRIN indexes.
